title: Time value of money and choosing projects
subtitle: A rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year. Put every cash flow on one date and the choice becomes arithmetic.

sections.title: Why money has a time value
sections.body: Money can be invested to earn a return, so Rs 1,000 today can become more later. Simple interest is earned only on the principal; compound interest earns interest on interest: F = P(1 + i)ⁿ. At 10 % for 5 years, Rs 1,000 grows to Rs 1,611; equivalently Rs 1,000 in 5 years is worth only Rs 621 today.

problems.prompt: How much will Rs 5,000 be worth in 8 years at 6 % compound interest?

sections.title: Equivalence and the cash-flow diagram
sections.body: Two cash flows are equivalent if they have the same worth at the same date and interest rate. A cash-flow diagram puts time on a horizontal axis, inflows as up arrows and outflows as down arrows. Below: invest 1,000 now and receive 350 at the end of each of 4 years, at MARR = 8 %.

Annuity A is a uniform end-of-period payment. The present worth of 350 a year for 4 years at 8 % is 1159.24; repaying a Rs 1,000 loan over 4 years costs 301.92 a year.

sections.title: Nominal and effective rates
sections.body: A nominal 12 % compounded monthly is 1 % per month; the effective annual rate is (1 + r/m)ᵐ − 1 = 12.68 %, more than 12 % because of within-year compounding. Always match the interest period to the payment period.

questions.prompt: Nominal 12 % compounded monthly has an effective rate that is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Interest on interest inside the year.

sections.title: Present worth and MARR
sections.body: The minimum attractive rate of return (MARR) is the least return the firm will accept. Project net present worth NPW = Σ Cₜ/(1 + MARR)ᵗ. If NPW > 0 the project earns more than MARR — accept. Project A at 8 %: NPW = −1000 + 350·(P/A) = 159.24; project B (invest 1,500, receive 500 a year) gives 156.06. Both are worth doing on their own; but only one can be built.

choices.text: The project earns more than the MARR: accept.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — project B
figures.note: Compare its present worth with project A.

sections.title: Internal rate of return
sections.body: The IRR is the rate that makes NPW = 0. Accept if IRR > MARR. Project A: IRR ≈ 14.96 %; project B: 12.59 %. Both beat 8 %. The IRR is found by trial (or by the card’s solver) — there is no closed form for n > 4.

worked.why: That is almost zero, so the IRR is just under 15 %.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Inflows exactly repay outflows with interest.

sections.title: Comparing alternatives: incremental analysis
sections.body: Only one of A, B can be built. The larger IRR does not always win, and a bigger investment is justified only if its extra money earns enough. Analyse the increment B − A: extra investment 500, extra return 150 a year, incremental IRR ≈ 7.71 %. That is below the MARR of 8 %, so the extra 500 is not worth spending: choose A. (Consistent with NPW(A) = 159.24 > NPW(B) = 156.06, even though B has the larger returns.) Compare equal-life options by NPW; unequal lives by annual worth, which repeats each as if replaced.

sections.title: Benefit–cost ratio and payback
sections.body: Public projects use B/C = PW(benefits)/PW(costs); accept if > 1. Payback is the time to recover the investment: simple payback for A = 1000/350 = 2.86 years. It ignores the time value and cash flows after payback, so use it only as a rough liquidity check.

questions.prompt: A weakness of simple payback is that it…

choices.text: Ignores the time value of money and later cash flows.
